Maker–Breaker · the Snaky hexomino · 758 proof cards · improved

Snaky in 20

The same game as Snaky in 21, but Black plays an improved strategy: the paper's cards plus 30 new ones, found by computer search and checked with the paper's own verifier. Black now always wins within 20 moves, and after a diagonal or knight's-move first reply within 18. How long can you make it take?

    Proof path

    Each step reads card:sXY: the card number, its symmetry s (bit 1 swaps x and y, bit 2 flips x, bit 4 flips y), and its offset XY in the paper's alphabet 0–9A–G. h is the most Black moves the card still needs. Hover a step for details.

      How Black thinks

      The paper proves the result with cards. A card is a promise of the form: if Black already owns the required cells A and White has no stone in the envelope T, Black wins within h more moves. Cards 0–5 are the six ways to be one stone from Snaky. Every later card plays one pivot stone and holds a hand of child cards whose envelopes have nothing in common except cells Black already owns. So whatever White replies, at least one child card survives, and its height is smaller.

      The final card here is 757. Like the paper's 727 it needs nothing (A = ∅) and fits in a 17×17 square, but it has height 20. Its pivot is tengen, K10. Of its children, single-stone cards of height 17 (new cards 738 and 749, in all their rotations) answer every diagonal and knight's-move reply, so those games end by move 18. Only a reply directly next to tengen keeps Black busy until move 20.

      Black follows its plan to the letter. It only ever plays the next stone of its current card and never looks for other ways to finish, so it can leave a ready win on the board for many moves. A perfect defence exploits this; the improved certificate adds cards that fit the extra stones Black happens to have, which is where the saved moves come from. In glass-box mode, a win Black has already passed over gets a green dashed ring.

      The paper's original 21-move strategy is at Snaky in 21.

      The squeeze

      Card 757 is a hand of placed cards: the paper's height-15 cards plus the new height-17 ones. Step through them and watch their common envelope shrink until only the pivot is left. That is why Black needs nothing to start.

      Credits
      
    
      
      
      The proof
      
      
      “Snaky in 21 Maker moves”,
        OpenAI, 25 September 2026, produced by an unreleased OpenAI model. The certificate Black plays here starts with its Appendix D, byte for byte, followed by 30 new cards that
        bring the bound to 20. The new cards are a draft: computer-checked, not yet reviewed by anyone else
        (how they were found and checked). 
      
      
      The method
      
      
      Nándor Sieben, whose proof trees for weak achievement games (Integers 8, 2008) are the direct ancestor of the cards,
        and whose Snaky is a 41-dimensional winner (2004) set out the problem’s history.
      
      
      The problem
      
      
      Frank Harary, who introduced polyomino achievement games.
        Harary, Harborth and Seemann, for handicap-two strategies.
        Immanuel Halupczok and Jan-Christoph Schlage-Puchta (Achieving Snaky, 2007): Snaky wins in three dimensions, loses on an 8×8 board, and has handicap number at most one.
        Hiro Ito and Hiromitsu Miyagawa: a handicap-one win (2007).
        András Csernenszky, Ryan R. Martin and András Pluhár: Breaker has no pairing defence (2011).
        Irfansha Shaik, Valentin Mayer-Eichberger, Jaco van de Pol and Abdallah Saffidine, and Steve Boucher and Roger Villemaire, for QBF encodings of these games.

      Designed and built by Claude (Anthropic) in Claude Code. Board, engine, heatmap and snake are plain JavaScript with no server.
